descripcion: Bronze helmet of the legion: open neck, cheek guards and a feather crest that identified the century.
Straight 60 cm sword with a flat blade and a point for stabbing: the legionary’s sword, not the long gladius of the movies.
Two-handled amphora for oil and wine, with the state’s seal on the neck: the packaging of imperial Rome.
Silver with the emperor’s effigy and a fineness that turned the state into the bank of the Mediterranean.
Marble slab with the biography of the deceased: cursus honorum, offices and epitaph. The most read text in the Roman world.
Funerary mask of solid gold with lapis and glass: the image of the pharaoh as a god, not as a portrait.
Clay vessels with vitreous glaze and painted decoration: the precision of the nilometer in every colour.
Medical papyrus of 1556 BC with 700 remedies: the oldest surviving physician’s handbook.
Wooden cradle with figures of goldsmiths, shell eyes and lapis: the most precious object of the Bronze Age.
Alabaster head from Uruk, one of the first representations of the human face in history.
Clay tablets with cuneiform writing: a complete administration recorded with a stylus.
Vase with black figures on a red ground, the glory of Athens: an entire industry in the service of Mediterranean trade.
Hermes of Kritios, the first figure to break free from the rigid block and discover contrapposto.
Bronze helmet with a crest of hair and cheek guards: the icon of the hoplites.
Basalt stele with the code of Hammurabi: 282 articles carved in Akkadian.
Cast bronze with the figure of a priest and the inscription of a casting recipe a thousand years old.
Jade sword with the inscription of the birds that identify the king: the objects of the Han court.
Steel folded in 15 layers, with the guard and the tsuka wrapped in silk.
Clay figures of warriors and animals that guarded the funerary gardens: the aesthetic of the Kofun.
Copper macehead with the unification scene: King Narmer strikes his enemies.
Coloured cords with knots that record accounting, and the census of the empire.
Jade mask of Tlaloc, god of rain, with the eye rings and the flint tongue.
Silver chalice with scenes of the life of Christ and of the imperial court: the splendour of the Byzantine world.
Tablet with a map of the Babylonian world and its asphalt roads, from 600 BC.
Viking steel axe with the mark of Loki, one of the few named weapons preserved.
Silver brooch with an animal head and interlaced nest motifs: the jewellery of ninth-century Vikings.
Golden bowl with the fabulous beasts of the imperial bestiary: the official art of the Achaemenid Empire.
Inscription in the three languages of the empire: the universal policy of Xerxes I.
Obsidian sword of Tizoc, on which the name of the Mexica emperor was carved.
Silver coin struck at Londinium with the image of Britannia: the mark of the Roman Empire.
